deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivation. It is a heavily corrected draft of the opening of a lecture course. Riemann's lectures on partial differential equations and their application to physical questions were later edited by K. Hattendorff (1869). The draft text is close to the published 'Einleitung' of that edition, with the overlap judged from memory of the printed text.

The argument, step by step:
(1) The subject of the course is the treatment of partial differential equations and their application to physical questions. Since no such lectures have yet been given in Göttingen, he will open with remarks on how the theory of PDEs relates to physics.
(2) Scientific physics really dates from the invention of the differential calculus. Only once one learned to follow the course of natural events continuously (reading uncertain) did attempts to reconstruct phenomena through concepts succeed. Newton created a few simple basic concepts and founded a method. That method derives, from simple elementary laws for single instants and points of space, the laws for finite times and spaces, which alone are accessible to observation.
(3) Galilei took the first step. He constructed the laws of free fall and of the action of gravity in individual instants, and so found the concept of the accelerating force, a simple cause of motion. Newton took the second step: the concept of an attracting action-at-a-distance, an elementary force. Physics still builds with these two basic concepts today.
(4) All attempts to go beyond these concepts into the 'interior of nature' have so far failed. As regards the basic concepts of physics, no new progress has been made since Newton.
(5) Method is different. There, progress has been made from laws valid for infinitely small time and space elements to laws valid for finite time intervals and distances. That is, from differential laws to their integrated, finite form, which is the role of the theory of differential equations.
(6) A marginal passage, largely illegible, apparently concerns the present state of mathematical specialisation and reducing phenomena to the two basic concepts.

My illustration, not on the page: the passage in (5) corresponds to going from a local law such as x''(t) = g to the finite law x(t) = x0 + v0*t + g*t^2/2. In field theory it corresponds to going from a PDE to its solution.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics. The historical framing simplifies matters: it credits Galilei with the 'concept of accelerating force' and makes action at a distance Newton's second basic concept. This is a standard 19th-century view of the history, not an error.

results.what: Programmatic statement that physics proceeds from elementary laws for infinitesimal space and time elements (differential equations) to finite laws by integration. Basic concepts: accelerating force (Galilei) and action at a distance (Newton).
results.modern_name: Methodological introduction to mathematical physics / PDEs (differential versus integral laws)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann himself, in the introduction to 'Partielle Differentialgleichungen und deren Anwendung auf physikalische Fragen' (ed. Hattendorff, 1869). The views are commonplace in 19th-century natural philosophy.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the introduction to Riemann's PDE lectures, whose printed version (Hattendorff 1869) already contains essentially these remarks on Galilei, Newton and the differential method. It has no mathematical content; only its value as a draft is of interest.

checkable.asserts: My illustration, not on the page. The infinitesimal law of free fall integrates to the finite law x = C1 + C2*t + g*t**2/2, the passage from instantaneous to finite laws described in the text.

transcription_corrections: Right margin next to the line about following the course of events: the insertion reads approximately 'Naturereignisse stetig zu', i.e. '...den Lauf der Naturereignisse stetig zu folgen/verfolgen'. The machine reading 'folgen zu folgen' drops 'stetig'.
The phrase 'in einzelnen Zeitpunkten construirte' matches the image, and 'allen' before it is struck out, as transcribed.
The heading at top right ('Gewisse methodische Bemerkung... schalten/finden') is very uncertain. It may read something like 'Gewisse methodische Bemerkungen einschalten'.

In 'die Gesetze für endliche (gedachte) Räume und Zeiten herzuleiten, welche allein der Beobachtung zugänglich sind', the second verb ('abzuleiten') seems to belong to a struck or alternative phrasing. The main text probably keeps only one of the two verbs.
The lower right marginal block (beginning 'Nach der heutigen mathematischen Specialisirung') is largely illegible in the image. The machine readings there should be treated as conjectural.
